<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[bn:বিদ্যারাজ]][[en:Wisdom King]][[es:Reyes de la sabiduría]][[eu:Vidyarāja]][[fr:Vidyaraja]][[hu:Bölcsességkirályok]][[id:Vidyārāja]][[ja:明王]][[ko:명왕]][[lt:Vidjaradža]][[pl:Widjaradża]][[ro:Regii înțelepciunii]][[ru:Видья-раджа]][[ta:வித்யாராஜாக்கள்]][[th:วิทยาราช]][[zh:明王]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q855113]] Wikidata name: Wisdom King [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:22, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Wrathful deity in East Asian Buddhism}} {{Vajrayana}}
A '''Wisdom King''' ([[:en:Sanskrit|Sanskrit]]: विद्याराज; [[:en:International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration|IAST]]: ''Vidyārāja'', {{cjkv|p=Míngwáng|c=明王|r=Myōō}}) is a type of [[:en:Wrathful deities|wrathful deity]] in [[:en:East Asian Buddhism|East Asian Buddhism]].
Whereas the Sanskrit name is translated literally as "wisdom / knowledge king(s)," the term ''[[:en:Vidya (philosophy)|vidyā]]'' in [[:en:Vajrayana Buddhism|Vajrayana Buddhism]] is also specifically used to denote [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]];<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Toganoo |first1=Shozui Makoto |title=The Symbol-System of Shingon Buddhism (1) |journal=Journal of Esoteric Buddhism – Mikkyō Bunka |date=1971 |pages=91, 86 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jeb1947/1971/96/1971_96_L95/_pdf/-char/ja}}</ref> the term may thus also be rendered "mantra king(s)."{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Mack|2006|p=298}} ''Vidyā'' is translated in Chinese with the character (lit. "bright, radiant", figuratively "knowledge(able), wisdom, wise"), leading to a wide array of alternative translations such as "bright king(s)" or "radiant king(s)". A similar Category of fierce deities known as [[:en:Heruka|Heruka]]s are found in [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan Buddhism]].
The female counterparts of Wisdom Kings are known as '''Wisdom Queens''' (Sanskrit (IAST): ''Vidyārājñī'', Chinese: 明妃, ''Míngfēi'', Japanese: ''Myōhi'').
===Development=== [[File:Dazu-Baoding Shan-304-No21-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|300px|Carved cliff relief of [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamantaka]] (''Dàwēidé Míngwáng)'', one out of a set depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings, at the [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|Dazu Rock Carvings]] in [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]]. 12th century. ]] ''Vidyārājas'', as their name suggests, are originally conceived of as the guardians and personifications of esoteric wisdom (''vidyā''), namely [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]] and [[:en:Dharani|Dharani]]s. They were seen as embodying the mystic power contained in these sacred utterances.{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=116}}
During the early stages of esoteric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, many of the deities that would become known as ''vidyārājas'' (a term that only came into use around the late 7th-early 8th century{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=90}}) were mainly seen as attendants of [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]]s who were invoked for specific ends such as the removal of misfortune and obstacles to [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. They personified certain attributes of these bodhisattvas such as their wisdom or the power of their voices and were held to perform various tasks such as gathering together sentient beings to whom the bodhisattva preaches, subjugating unruly elements, or protecting adherents of Buddhism.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13, 64-65}} Eventually, these divinities became objects of veneration in their own right; no longer necessarily paired with a bodhisattva, they became considered as the manifestations of the bodhisattvas themselves and/or of [[:en:Buddhahood|buddhas]], who are believed to assume terrifying forms as a [[:en:Upaya|means]] to save sentient beings out of [[:en:Karuṇā|compassion]] for them.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13}} A belief prevalent in the Japanese tradition known as the ''sanrinjin'' (三輪身, "bodies of the three wheels") theory for instance posits that five Wisdom Kings are the fierce incarnations (教令輪身, ''kyōryōrin-shin'', lit. "embodiments of the wheel of injunction") of the [[:en:Five Tathāgatas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]], who appear both as gentle bodhisattvas who teach the Dharma through compassion and as terrifying ''vidyārājas'' who teach through fear, shocking nonbelievers into faith.{{sfnp|Baroni|2002|p=100}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|2006|p=56}}<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_H5p-Fqkuz8C&pg=PA120|title=昭和新纂国訳大蔵経 解説部第1巻 (Shōwa shinsan Kokuyaku Daizōkyō: Kaisetsu, vol. 1)|date=1930|publisher=Tōhō Shuppan|pages=120|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=三輪身|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E8%BC%AA%E8%BA%AB-71616|access-date=2020-11-28|website=コトバンク (kotobank)|language=ja}}</ref>
[[File:Indian Museum Sculpture - Manjusri, 10c, Kurkihar (9220688818).jpg|thumb|150px|[[Manjushri]] with Yamāntaka, from Kurkihar ([[:en:Bihar|Bihar]]), currently at the [[:en:Indian Museum, Kolkata|Indian Museum]] in [[:en:Kolkata|Kolkata]]. 10th century.|left]] The evolution of the ''vidyārāja'' will be illustrated here by the deity [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]], one of the earliest Buddhist wrathful deities. In the 6th century text ''[[:en:Manjushrimulakalpa|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa]]'', Yamāntaka is portrayed as the oath-bound servant of the bodhisattva [[Manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] who assembles all beings from across the world to hear the Buddha's preaching and vanquishes (and converts) those who are hostile to Buddhism; at the same time, Yamāntaka is also the personification of Mañjuśrī's dharani, the benefits of which are identical to his abilities.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=64-67}} He was also commonly depicted in statuary along with Mañjuśrī as a diminutive [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]]-like attendant figure.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=68-81}}
[[File:Dai Itoku Myoo Yamantaka Toji.JPG|thumb|Yamāntaka (''Daiitoku Myōō''), at [[Tō-ji]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (13th or 14th century). ]] Later, as Yamāntaka and similar subordinates of various bodhisattvas (e.g. [[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]], who was associated with [[:en:Avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]]) became fully independent deities, they began to be portrayed by themselves and increasingly acquired iconographic attributes specific to each. Yamāntaka for instance is commonly shown with six heads, arms, and legs and riding or standing on a [[:en:Water Buffalo|buffalo]] [[:en:Vahana|mount]].{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} The status and function of these deities have shifted from being minor emissaries who gather together and intimidate recalcitrant beings to being intimately involved in the primary task of esoteric Buddhism: the transformation of passions and ignorance (''[[:en:Avidyā (Buddhism)|avidyā]]'') into compassion and wisdom.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=155}} As a result of this development, the relationship between Mañjuśrī and Yamāntaka was recontextualized such that Yamāntaka is now considered to be the incarnation of Mañjuśrī himself (so the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|Mañjuśrī-nāma-samgīti]]'').{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} Eventually, in the ''sanrinjin'' interpretation of Japanese esoteric Buddhism, both Yamāntaka and Mañjuśrī - under the name 'Vajratīkṣṇa' (Japanese: 金剛利菩薩, ''Kongōri Bosatsu'')<ref>{{cite web |title=3. 両界曼荼羅（りょうかいまんだら） |url=https://ermjp.com/j/temple/mandara/manda/oshie/oshie7.html |website=Shingon-shū Sennyū-ji-ha Jōdo-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Vajratiksna |url=https://english-tibetan-dictionary.tumblr.com/post/59668575364/vajratiksna |website=English Tibetan Dictionary Online |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref> - became classified as avatars of the buddha [[Amitābha|Amitābha]].<ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A7%E5%A8%81%E5%BE%B3%E6%98%8E%E7%8E%8B-90795 |website=コトバンク (Kotobank) |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=http://www.ict.ne.jp/~jofukuji/daiitoku.html |website=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha Kōki-zan Jōfuku-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref>
Other Wisdom Kings followed a more or less similar development. Hayagrīva, for example, was originally the horse-headed incarnation of the [[:en:Hinduism|Hindu]] god [[:en:Vishnu|Vishnu]] which was adopted into Buddhism as Avalokiteśvara's attendant (although unlike the Hindu [[:en:Hayagriva|Hayagrīva]], the Buddhist figure was never portrayed with a horse's head, instead being depicted like Yamāntaka as a yaksha who may have a miniature horse head emerging from his hair).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=85-91}} Eventually, as Hayagrīva increasingly rose to prominence, the distinction between him and his superior became increasingly blurred so that he ultimately turned into one of Avalokiteśvara's many guises in both China and Japan.{{sfnp|Chandra|1988|pp=29-31}} One of the more famous ''vidyārājas'', [[Acala]] (Acalanātha), was originally an acolyte or messenger of the buddha [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]] before he was interpreted as Vairocana's fierce aspect or ''kyōryōrin-shin'' in the Japanese tradition.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=120-123}} (In Nepal and Tibet, meanwhile, he is instead identified as the incarnation of either Mañjuśrī or the buddha [[Akshobhya|Akṣobhya]].{{sfnp|Pal|1974|p=6}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Acala, The Buddhist Protector|url=https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38011|access-date=2020-11-28|website=Metropolitan Museum of Art}}</ref>{{sfnp|Jha|1993|pp=35–36}}<ref name=":22">{{Cite web|title=Sacred Visions: Early Paintings from Central Tibet - Achala|url=https://www.asianart.com/exhibitions/svision/i22.html|access-date=2020-11-28|website=www.asianart.com}}</ref>)
==Iconography== {{multiple image | direction = vertical | width = 200 | footer = | image1 = Kongosanmaiin tahoto interior.jpg | caption1 = Statues of the [[:en:Five Tathāgatas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]] (五智如来, ''Gochi Nyorai'') at [[:en:Kongō Sanmai-in|Kongō Sanmai-in]] in [[:en:Mount Kōya|Mount Kōya]], Japan. Kamakura period (13th century). Clockwise starting from the front right: [[Amoghasiddhi]], [[Akshobhya]], [[:en:Ratnasambhava|Ratnasambhava]], and [[Amitābha|Amitabha]]. [[:en:Vairochana|Vairochana]] is at the center. | image2 = The Five Wisdom Kings.jpg | caption2 = The Five Wisdom Kings (五大明王, ''Godai Myōō''). Clockwise starting from the top right: [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]], [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]], [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]], and [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]]. [[Acala]] is at the center. }}
The iconography of Buddhist wrathful deities are usually considered to be derived from both [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] imagery and [[:en:Shaivism|Shaivite]] iconography, specifically from the wrathful forms of the Hindu god [[:en:Shiva|Shiva]] (e.g. [[:en:Bhairava|Bhairava]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=330}}<ref>{{Cite web|last=Van Hartingsveldt|first=Michael|date=2018-09-21|title=With the Wrath of a Serpent: The Propagation of Gundari Myо̄о̄ Iconography|url=https://www.buddhistdoor.net/features/with-the-wrath-of-a-serpent-the-propagation-of-gudari-myoo-iconography|access-date=2021-09-25|website=Buddhistdoor Global}}</ref>
Wisdom Kings are usually represented as fierce-looking, often with blue or black skin and multiple heads, arms, and legs. They hold various weapons in their hands and are sometimes adorned with [[Mundamala|skulls]], [[Shiva#Attributes|snakes or animal skins]] and wreathed in flames. This fiery aura is symbolically interpreted as the fire that purifies the practitioner and transforms one's [[:en:Kleshas (Buddhism)|passions]] into awakening, the so-called "fire ''[[Samadhi#Samādhi|samadhi]]''" (火生三昧, Japanese: ''kashō-zanmai'').{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=117}}
Certain ''vidyārājas'' bear attributes that reflect [[Decline of Buddhism in the Indian subcontinent#Religious competition|the historical rivalry]] between Hinduism and Buddhism. For instance, the Wisdom King [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] is shown defeating and trampling on the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Maheshvara|Maheśvara]] (one of the Buddhist analogues to Shiva) and his consort Umā ([[:en:Parvati|Pārvatī]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=178-187}} A commentary on the ''[[:en:Mahavairocana Tantra|Mahavairocana Tantra]]'' by the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] monk [[Yi Xing]] meanwhile attributes the taming of Maheśvara to another ''vidyārāja'', Acala.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=124-125}} Acala himself is sometimes shown trampling on an elephant-headed demon/deity [[Kangiten#Historical development and literature|who may share a common origin]] with the Hindu [[:en:Ganesha|Ganesha]] named Vighnarāja (the "Lord of Obstacles") in [[:en:Tibetan art|Tibetan art]].{{sfnp|Faure|2015b|pp=47, 94–98}}
==List of Wisdom Kings== ===The Five Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese]] and Japanese ([[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon]] and [[:en:Tendai|Tendai]]) esoteric Buddhism, the '''Five Great Wisdom Kings''' (五大明王, Jp. ''Godai Myōō''; Ch. ''Wǔ Dà Míngwáng''), also known as the '''Five Guardian Kings''', are a group of ''vidyārājas'' who are considered to be both the fierce emanations of the [[:en:Five Wisdom Buddhas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]] and the guardians of Buddhist doctrine.{{sfnp|De Visser|1928|pp=143-151}}<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vilbar |first1=Sinéad |title=Kings of Brightness in Japanese Esoteric Buddhist Art |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/kibr/hd_kibr.htm |website=The Metropolitan Museum of Art |access-date=2021-10-01 |date=October 2013}}</ref> Organized according to the five directions (the [[:en:Cardinal direction|four cardinal points]] plus the center), the Five Kings are usually defined as follows:
* [[Acala|Acala / Acalanātha]] (不動明王; Jp. ''Fudō Myōō''; Ch. 不動明王, ''Bùdòng Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Vairocana|Mahāvairocana]], associated with the center * [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (降三世明王; Jp. ''Gōzanze Myōō''; Ch. ''Xiángsānshì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Akshobhya|Akshobhya]], associated with the east * [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali / Amṛtakuṇḍalin]] (軍荼利明王, Jp. ''Gundari Myōō''; Ch. ''Jūntúlì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Ratnasambhava|Ratnasambhava]], associated with the south * [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (大威徳明王; Jp. ''Daiitoku Myōō''; Ch. ''Dàwēidé Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amitābha]], associated with the west * [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]] (金剛夜叉明王, Jp. ''Kongōyasha Myōō''; Ch. ''Jīngāng Yèchā Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amoghasiddhi]], associated with the north in the Shingon school ** [[:en:Ucchusma|Ucchuṣma]] (烏枢沙摩明王; Jp. ''Ususama Myōō''; Ch. ''Wūshūshāmó Míngwáng'') - Associated with the north in the Tendai school<ref>{{cite web |title=五大尊 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/5daison/index.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudō (Ryukō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-01}}</ref>

===The Eight Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|Chinese Buddhism]], the '''Eight Great Wisdom Kings''' (八大明王; pinyin: ''Bā Dà Míngwáng''), is another grouping of Wisdom Kings that is depicted in statues, mural art and paintings. The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping of eight is the ''Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa'', the Chinese translation of which (大方廣菩薩藏文殊舍利根本儀軌經; ''Dà fāngguǎng Púsà Zàng Wénshūshèlì Gēnběn Yíguǐ Jīng'', lit. "The Fundamental Ordinance of Mañjuśrī") in about 980-1000 CE is attributed to the monk Tianxizai, who is possibly the north Indian [[:en:Shantideva|Shantideva]].{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} Each of the Wisdom Kings correspond to one of the [[Eight Great Bodhisattvas]][[:zh:八大菩萨|<sup>zh]</sup>]] in Chinese Buddhism as well as to a specific compass direction.
The Eight Wisdom Kings, with exceptions in certain lists, are usually defined as:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} * Acala - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin|Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin]], associated with the north-east * Kuṇḍali - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Ākāśagarbha|Ākāśagarbha]], associated with the north-west * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrapani|Vajrapāṇi]], associated with the south-east *[[Mahācakra]] (大輪明王; Ch. ''Dàlún Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[Maitreya]], associated with the south-west *[[Padanakṣipa]] (步擲明王; Ch. ''Bùzhì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], associated with the north *[[Aparājita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (無能勝明王; Ch. ''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Kṣitigarbha]], associated with the south *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, associated with the east *Hayagrīva (馬頭觀音; Ch. ''Mǎtóu Guānyīn'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]] ([[Kannon|Guanyin]]), associated with the west
{| align="center" border="0" cellspacing="5" |align = "center"|[[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (north-west) |align = "center"|[[Padanakṣipa]] (north) |align = "center"|[[Acala]] (north-east) |- |align = "center"|[[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]] (west) | |align = "center"|[[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (east) |- |align = "center"|[[Mahacakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (south-west) |align = "center"|[[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (south) |align = "center"|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (south-east) |}
=== The Ten Wisdom Kings === [[File:Dazu 2007 774.jpg|thumb|320px|The Wisdom Kings [[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparajita]] (''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng''; left), [[Mahācakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (''Dàlún Míngwáng''; center), and [[Padanakṣipa]] (''Bùzhì Míngwáng''; right). Part of a series of [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|rock carvings]] depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings in [[:en:Dazu District|Dazu District]], [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]].]]
Another grouping found in certain Chinese depictions is the '''Ten Great Wisdom Kings''' (十大明王; ''Shí Dà Míngwáng''). The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping is from ''The Sutra of the Liturgy for Brilliant Contemplation of the Ten Wrathful Wisdom Kings of the Illusory Net of the Great Yoga Teachings'' (佛說幻化網大瑜伽教十忿怒明王大明觀想儀軌經; ''Fóshuō Huànhuàwǎng Dà yújiājiào Shífènnù Míngwáng Dàmíng Guānxiǎng Yíguǐ Jīng)''.{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} There are several different groupings of the ten Kings, which differ in the removal and addition of certain ''vidyārājas'', as well as attributing some Kings to different buddhas and bodhisattvas. In medieval and modern Chinese Buddhist practice, the Ten Kings are regularly invoked in repentance ceremonies, such as the [[:en:Liberation Rite of Water and Land|Liberation Rite of Water and Land]], where they are offered offerings and entreated to expel evil from the ritual platform.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Bloom |first1=Phillip Emmanual |date=2013 |title=Descent of the Deities: The Water-Land Retreat and the Transformation of the Visual Culture of Song-Dynasty (960–1279) Buddhism |id={{ProQuest|1422026705}} |oclc=864907811 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hong |first1=Tsai-Hsia |title=The Water-Land Dharma Function Platform Ritual and the Great Compassion Repentance Ritual |date=2005 |oclc=64281400 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref>
One version of the list of Ten Wisdom Kings are as follows:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}}
* Acala - Manifestation of Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of Vajrapani *Mahācakra - Manifestation of Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Manifestation of Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Manifestation of Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of Amitābha *Hayagrīva - Manifestation of Avalokiteśvara *[[Vajrahāsa]] (大笑明王; Ch. ''Dàxiào Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of Ākāśagarbha *Ucchuṣma (穢跡金剛明王; Ch. ''Huìjì Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Vajra Being of Impure Traces") - Manifestation of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Śakyamuni]] *Ucchuṣma (?) (火頭金剛明王; Ch. ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Fire-Headed Vajra Being") - Manifestation of Mahāvairocana{{efn|''Huìjì Jīngāng'' and ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng'' are sometimes considered to be different names for the same figure, but at times are also regarded as two separate deities.}}
Another version of the list identifies the ten Kings with different buddhas and bodhisattvas:
*Acala - Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin *Kuṇḍali - Amitābha *Trailokyavijaya - Vajrapāṇi *Mahācakra - Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Mañjuśrī *Hayagrīva - Avalokiteśvara *Vajrahāsa - Ākāśagarbha *[[Mahabala (Wisdom King)|Mahābala]] (大力明王; Ch, ''Dàlì Míngwáng'') - Śakyamuni

===Others=== [[File:愛染明王, Rāgarāja, Kamakura period 2.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (''Aizen Myōō''), 13th century, Japan. [[:en:Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]]]
Other deities to whom the title ''vidyārāja'' is applied include:
* [[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (愛染明王; Ch. ''Àirǎn Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Aizen Myōō'') - A ''vidyaraja'' considered to transform worldly lust and sexual passion into spiritual awakening; manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrasattva|Vajrasattva]] and/or the buddha Vairochana.<ref>{{cite web |title=愛染明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/aizen.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref> * [[:en:Āṭavaka|Āṭavaka]] (大元帥明王; Ch. ''Dàyuánshuài Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daigensui Myōō'' or 大元明王, ''Daigen Myōō'') - A yaksha attendant of the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Vaiśravaṇa|Vaishravana]]. * [[Mahamayuri|Mahāmāyūrī]] (孔雀明王; Ch. ''Kǒngquè Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Kujaku Myōō'') - A Wisdom Queen (''vidyārājñī''); sometimes also classified as a bodhisattva. Unlike most other ''vidyārājas'', s/he is depicted with a benevolent expression. *Mahākrodharāja (大可畏明王; Ch. ''Dàkěwèi Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daikai Myōō'') - Attendant or manifestation of Amoghapasha (不空羂索観音; Ch. ''Bùkōng Juànsuǒ Guānyīn''; Jp. ''Fukū Kensaku/Kenjaku Kannon''), one of Avalokiteshvara's forms.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=89}}<ref>{{cite web |title=仏像がわかる！ バックナンバー４・明王部 |url=http://www5a.biglobe.ne.jp/~houon/butu-bk04.htm |website=Kōya-san Shingon-shū Hōon-in Official Website |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=不空大可畏明王央俱拾真言 |url=https://wisdombox.org/Mantra/15_t.pdf |website=JBox-智慧宝箧 |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref> *Sadākṣara (六字明王; Ch. ''Liùzì Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Rokuji Myōō'') - A deification of the Sadākṣara (Six-Letter) Sutra Ritual (六字経法; Jp. ''Rokuji-kyō hō''), a rite of subjugation focused on the [[Guanyin#Manifestations of Guanyin|six manifestations]] of Avalokiteshvara.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fuji |first1=Tatsuhiko |title=呪法全書 (Juhō Zensho) |date=2012 |publisher=Gakken Plus |isbn=978-4-0591-1008-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gi5jCwAAQBAJ&pg=PT150}}</ref> Unlike other Wisdom Kings but like Mahamayuri, he sports a gentle bodhisattva-like countenance and is shown with four or six arms and standing on one leg.<ref>{{cite web |title=円成庵 木造六字尊立像 |url=http://www.sumitomo.or.jp/html/culja/culja17/jp17029.htm |website=2017th year 度 文化財維持・修復事業助成 助成対象 |publisher=The Sumitomo Foundation|access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=木造六字明王立像 |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/kurashi/kosodate/bunka/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai/chokoku/rokujison_ritsuzo.html |website=Takamatsu City Official Website |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=六字明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/rokuji.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[bn:বিদ্যারাজ]][[en:Wisdom King]][[es:Reyes de la sabiduría]][[eu:Vidyarāja]][[fr:Vidyaraja]][[hu:Bölcsességkirályok]][[id:Vidyārāja]][[ja:明王]][[ko:명왕]][[lt:Vidjaradža]][[pl:Widjaradża]][[ro:Regii înțelepciunii]][[ru:Видья-раджа]][[ta:வித்யாராஜாக்கள்]][[th:วิทยาราช]][[zh:明王]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q855113]] Wikidata name: Wisdom King [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:22, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Wrathful deity in East Asian Buddhism}} {{Vajrayana}}
A '''Wisdom King''' ([[:en:Sanskrit|Sanskrit]]: विद्याराज; [[:en:International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration|IAST]]: ''Vidyārāja'', {{cjkv|p=Míngwáng|c=明王|r=Myōō}}) is a type of [[:en:Wrathful deities|wrathful deity]] in [[:en:East Asian Buddhism|East Asian Buddhism]].
Whereas the Sanskrit name is translated literally as "wisdom / knowledge king(s)," the term ''[[:en:Vidya (philosophy)|vidyā]]'' in [[:en:Vajrayana Buddhism|Vajrayana Buddhism]] is also specifically used to denote [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]];<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Toganoo |first1=Shozui Makoto |title=The Symbol-System of Shingon Buddhism (1) |journal=Journal of Esoteric Buddhism – Mikkyō Bunka |date=1971 |pages=91, 86 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jeb1947/1971/96/1971_96_L95/_pdf/-char/ja}}</ref> the term may thus also be rendered "mantra king(s)."{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Mack|2006|p=298}} ''Vidyā'' is translated in Chinese with the character (lit. "bright, radiant", figuratively "knowledge(able), wisdom, wise"), leading to a wide array of alternative translations such as "bright king(s)" or "radiant king(s)". A similar Category of fierce deities known as [[:en:Heruka|Heruka]]s are found in [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan Buddhism]].
The female counterparts of Wisdom Kings are known as '''Wisdom Queens''' (Sanskrit (IAST): ''Vidyārājñī'', Chinese: 明妃, ''Míngfēi'', Japanese: ''Myōhi'').
===Development=== [[File:Dazu-Baoding Shan-304-No21-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|300px|Carved cliff relief of [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamantaka]] (''Dàwēidé Míngwáng)'', one out of a set depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings, at the [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|Dazu Rock Carvings]] in [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]]. 12th century. ]] ''Vidyārājas'', as their name suggests, are originally conceived of as the guardians and personifications of esoteric wisdom (''vidyā''), namely [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]] and [[:en:Dharani|Dharani]]s. They were seen as embodying the mystic power contained in these sacred utterances.{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=116}}
During the early stages of esoteric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, many of the deities that would become known as ''vidyārājas'' (a term that only came into use around the late 7th-early 8th century{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=90}}) were mainly seen as attendants of [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]]s who were invoked for specific ends such as the removal of misfortune and obstacles to [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. They personified certain attributes of these bodhisattvas such as their wisdom or the power of their voices and were held to perform various tasks such as gathering together sentient beings to whom the bodhisattva preaches, subjugating unruly elements, or protecting adherents of Buddhism.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13, 64-65}} Eventually, these divinities became objects of veneration in their own right; no longer necessarily paired with a bodhisattva, they became considered as the manifestations of the bodhisattvas themselves and/or of [[:en:Buddhahood|buddhas]], who are believed to assume terrifying forms as a [[:en:Upaya|means]] to save sentient beings out of [[:en:Karuṇā|compassion]] for them.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13}} A belief prevalent in the Japanese tradition known as the ''sanrinjin'' (三輪身, "bodies of the three wheels") theory for instance posits that five Wisdom Kings are the fierce incarnations (教令輪身, ''kyōryōrin-shin'', lit. "embodiments of the wheel of injunction") of the [[:en:Five Tathāgatas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]], who appear both as gentle bodhisattvas who teach the Dharma through compassion and as terrifying ''vidyārājas'' who teach through fear, shocking nonbelievers into faith.{{sfnp|Baroni|2002|p=100}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|2006|p=56}}<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_H5p-Fqkuz8C&pg=PA120|title=昭和新纂国訳大蔵経 解説部第1巻 (Shōwa shinsan Kokuyaku Daizōkyō: Kaisetsu, vol. 1)|date=1930|publisher=Tōhō Shuppan|pages=120|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=三輪身|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E8%BC%AA%E8%BA%AB-71616|access-date=2020-11-28|website=コトバンク (kotobank)|language=ja}}</ref>
[[File:Indian Museum Sculpture - Manjusri, 10c, Kurkihar (9220688818).jpg|thumb|150px|[[Manjushri]] with Yamāntaka, from Kurkihar ([[:en:Bihar|Bihar]]), currently at the [[:en:Indian Museum, Kolkata|Indian Museum]] in [[:en:Kolkata|Kolkata]]. 10th century.|left]] The evolution of the ''vidyārāja'' will be illustrated here by the deity [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]], one of the earliest Buddhist wrathful deities. In the 6th century text ''[[:en:Manjushrimulakalpa|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa]]'', Yamāntaka is portrayed as the oath-bound servant of the bodhisattva [[Manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] who assembles all beings from across the world to hear the Buddha's preaching and vanquishes (and converts) those who are hostile to Buddhism; at the same time, Yamāntaka is also the personification of Mañjuśrī's dharani, the benefits of which are identical to his abilities.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=64-67}} He was also commonly depicted in statuary along with Mañjuśrī as a diminutive [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]]-like attendant figure.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=68-81}}
[[File:Dai Itoku Myoo Yamantaka Toji.JPG|thumb|Yamāntaka (''Daiitoku Myōō''), at [[Tō-ji]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (13th or 14th century). ]] Later, as Yamāntaka and similar subordinates of various bodhisattvas (e.g. [[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]], who was associated with [[:en:Avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]]) became fully independent deities, they began to be portrayed by themselves and increasingly acquired iconographic attributes specific to each. Yamāntaka for instance is commonly shown with six heads, arms, and legs and riding or standing on a [[:en:Water Buffalo|buffalo]] [[:en:Vahana|mount]].{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} The status and function of these deities have shifted from being minor emissaries who gather together and intimidate recalcitrant beings to being intimately involved in the primary task of esoteric Buddhism: the transformation of passions and ignorance (''[[:en:Avidyā (Buddhism)|avidyā]]'') into compassion and wisdom.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=155}} As a result of this development, the relationship between Mañjuśrī and Yamāntaka was recontextualized such that Yamāntaka is now considered to be the incarnation of Mañjuśrī himself (so the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|Mañjuśrī-nāma-samgīti]]'').{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} Eventually, in the ''sanrinjin'' interpretation of Japanese esoteric Buddhism, both Yamāntaka and Mañjuśrī - under the name 'Vajratīkṣṇa' (Japanese: 金剛利菩薩, ''Kongōri Bosatsu'')<ref>{{cite web |title=3. 両界曼荼羅（りょうかいまんだら） |url=https://ermjp.com/j/temple/mandara/manda/oshie/oshie7.html |website=Shingon-shū Sennyū-ji-ha Jōdo-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Vajratiksna |url=https://english-tibetan-dictionary.tumblr.com/post/59668575364/vajratiksna |website=English Tibetan Dictionary Online |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref> - became classified as avatars of the buddha [[Amitābha|Amitābha]].<ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A7%E5%A8%81%E5%BE%B3%E6%98%8E%E7%8E%8B-90795 |website=コトバンク (Kotobank) |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=http://www.ict.ne.jp/~jofukuji/daiitoku.html |website=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha Kōki-zan Jōfuku-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref>
Other Wisdom Kings followed a more or less similar development. Hayagrīva, for example, was originally the horse-headed incarnation of the [[:en:Hinduism|Hindu]] god [[:en:Vishnu|Vishnu]] which was adopted into Buddhism as Avalokiteśvara's attendant (although unlike the Hindu [[:en:Hayagriva|Hayagrīva]], the Buddhist figure was never portrayed with a horse's head, instead being depicted like Yamāntaka as a yaksha who may have a miniature horse head emerging from his hair).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=85-91}} Eventually, as Hayagrīva increasingly rose to prominence, the distinction between him and his superior became increasingly blurred so that he ultimately turned into one of Avalokiteśvara's many guises in both China and Japan.{{sfnp|Chandra|1988|pp=29-31}} One of the more famous ''vidyārājas'', [[Acala]] (Acalanātha), was originally an acolyte or messenger of the buddha [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]] before he was interpreted as Vairocana's fierce aspect or ''kyōryōrin-shin'' in the Japanese tradition.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=120-123}} (In Nepal and Tibet, meanwhile, he is instead identified as the incarnation of either Mañjuśrī or the buddha [[Akshobhya|Akṣobhya]].{{sfnp|Pal|1974|p=6}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Acala, The Buddhist Protector|url=https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38011|access-date=2020-11-28|website=Metropolitan Museum of Art}}</ref>{{sfnp|Jha|1993|pp=35–36}}<ref name=":22">{{Cite web|title=Sacred Visions: Early Paintings from Central Tibet - Achala|url=https://www.asianart.com/exhibitions/svision/i22.html|access-date=2020-11-28|website=www.asianart.com}}</ref>)

[[:en:Vairochana|Vairochana]] is at the center. | image2 = The Five Wisdom Kings.jpg | caption2 = The Five Wisdom Kings (五大明王, ''Godai Myōō''). Clockwise starting from the top right: [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]], [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]], [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]], and [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]]. [[Acala]] is at the center. }}
The iconography of Buddhist wrathful deities are usually considered to be derived from both [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] imagery and [[:en:Shaivism|Shaivite]] iconography, specifically from the wrathful forms of the Hindu god [[:en:Shiva|Shiva]] (e.g. [[:en:Bhairava|Bhairava]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=330}}<ref>{{Cite web|last=Van Hartingsveldt|first=Michael|date=2018-09-21|title=With the Wrath of a Serpent: The Propagation of Gundari Myо̄о̄ Iconography|url=https://www.buddhistdoor.net/features/with-the-wrath-of-a-serpent-the-propagation-of-gudari-myoo-iconography|access-date=2021-09-25|website=Buddhistdoor Global}}</ref>
Wisdom Kings are usually represented as fierce-looking, often with blue or black skin and multiple heads, arms, and legs. They hold various weapons in their hands and are sometimes adorned with [[Mundamala|skulls]], [[Shiva#Attributes|snakes or animal skins]] and wreathed in flames. This fiery aura is symbolically interpreted as the fire that purifies the practitioner and transforms one's [[:en:Kleshas (Buddhism)|passions]] into awakening, the so-called "fire ''[[Samadhi#Samādhi|samadhi]]''" (火生三昧, Japanese: ''kashō-zanmai'').{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=117}}
Certain ''vidyārājas'' bear attributes that reflect [[Decline of Buddhism in the Indian subcontinent#Religious competition|the historical rivalry]] between Hinduism and Buddhism. For instance, the Wisdom King [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] is shown defeating and trampling on the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Maheshvara|Maheśvara]] (one of the Buddhist analogues to Shiva) and his consort Umā ([[:en:Parvati|Pārvatī]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=178-187}} A commentary on the ''[[:en:Mahavairocana Tantra|Mahavairocana Tantra]]'' by the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] monk [[Yi Xing]] meanwhile attributes the taming of Maheśvara to another ''vidyārāja'', Acala.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=124-125}} Acala himself is sometimes shown trampling on an elephant-headed demon/deity [[Kangiten#Historical development and literature|who may share a common origin]] with the Hindu [[:en:Ganesha|Ganesha]] named Vighnarāja (the "Lord of Obstacles") in [[:en:Tibetan art|Tibetan art]].{{sfnp|Faure|2015b|pp=47, 94–98}}
==List of Wisdom Kings== ===The Five Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese]] and Japanese ([[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon]] and [[:en:Tendai|Tendai]]) esoteric Buddhism, the '''Five Great Wisdom Kings''' (五大明王, Jp. ''Godai Myōō''; Ch. ''Wǔ Dà Míngwáng''), also known as the '''Five Guardian Kings''', are a group of ''vidyārājas'' who are considered to be both the fierce emanations of the [[:en:Five Wisdom Buddhas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]] and the guardians of Buddhist doctrine.{{sfnp|De Visser|1928|pp=143-151}}<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vilbar |first1=Sinéad |title=Kings of Brightness in Japanese Esoteric Buddhist Art |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/kibr/hd_kibr.htm |website=The Metropolitan Museum of Art |access-date=2021-10-01 |date=October 2013}}</ref> Organized according to the five directions (the [[:en:Cardinal direction|four cardinal points]] plus the center), the Five Kings are usually defined as follows:
* [[Acala|Acala / Acalanātha]] (不動明王; Jp. ''Fudō Myōō''; Ch. 不動明王, ''Bùdòng Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Vairocana|Mahāvairocana]], associated with the center * [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (降三世明王; Jp. ''Gōzanze Myōō''; Ch. ''Xiángsānshì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Akshobhya|Akshobhya]], associated with the east * [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali / Amṛtakuṇḍalin]] (軍荼利明王, Jp. ''Gundari Myōō''; Ch. ''Jūntúlì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Ratnasambhava|Ratnasambhava]], associated with the south * [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (大威徳明王; Jp. ''Daiitoku Myōō''; Ch. ''Dàwēidé Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amitābha]], associated with the west * [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]] (金剛夜叉明王, Jp. ''Kongōyasha Myōō''; Ch. ''Jīngāng Yèchā Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amoghasiddhi]], associated with the north in the Shingon school ** [[:en:Ucchusma|Ucchuṣma]] (烏枢沙摩明王; Jp. ''Ususama Myōō''; Ch. ''Wūshūshāmó Míngwáng'') - Associated with the north in the Tendai school<ref>{{cite web |title=五大尊 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/5daison/index.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudō (Ryukō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-01}}</ref>
{| align="center" border="0" cellspacing="5" | |align = "center"|[[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]] ''or'' [[:en:Ucchusma|Ucchuṣma]] (north) | |- |align = "center"|[[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]] (west) |align = "center"|[[Acala]] (center) |align = "center"|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (east) |- | |align = "center"|[[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (south) | |}
===The Eight Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|Chinese Buddhism]], the '''Eight Great Wisdom Kings''' (八大明王; pinyin: ''Bā Dà Míngwáng''), is another grouping of Wisdom Kings that is depicted in statues, mural art and paintings. The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping of eight is the ''Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa'', the Chinese translation of which (大方廣菩薩藏文殊舍利根本儀軌經; ''Dà fāngguǎng Púsà Zàng Wénshūshèlì Gēnběn Yíguǐ Jīng'', lit. "The Fundamental Ordinance of Mañjuśrī") in about 980-1000 CE is attributed to the monk Tianxizai, who is possibly the north Indian [[:en:Shantideva|Shantideva]].{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} Each of the Wisdom Kings correspond to one of the [[Eight Great Bodhisattvas]][[:zh:八大菩萨|<sup>zh]</sup>]] in Chinese Buddhism as well as to a specific compass direction.
The Eight Wisdom Kings, with exceptions in certain lists, are usually defined as:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} * Acala - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin|Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin]], associated with the north-east * Kuṇḍali - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Ākāśagarbha|Ākāśagarbha]], associated with the north-west * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrapani|Vajrapāṇi]], associated with the south-east *[[Mahācakra]] (大輪明王; Ch. ''Dàlún Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[Maitreya]], associated with the south-west *[[Padanakṣipa]] (步擲明王; Ch. ''Bùzhì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], associated with the north *[[Aparājita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (無能勝明王; Ch. ''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Kṣitigarbha]], associated with the south *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, associated with the east *Hayagrīva (馬頭觀音; Ch. ''Mǎtóu Guānyīn'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]] ([[Kannon|Guanyin]]), associated with the west
{| align="center" border="0" cellspacing="5" |align = "center"|[[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (north-west) |align = "center"|[[Padanakṣipa]] (north) |align = "center"|[[Acala]] (north-east) |- |align = "center"|[[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]] (west) | |align = "center"|[[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (east) |- |align = "center"|[[Mahacakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (south-west) |align = "center"|[[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (south) |align = "center"|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (south-east) |}
=== The Ten Wisdom Kings === [[File:Dazu 2007 774.jpg|thumb|320px|The Wisdom Kings [[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparajita]] (''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng''; left), [[Mahācakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (''Dàlún Míngwáng''; center), and [[Padanakṣipa]] (''Bùzhì Míngwáng''; right). Part of a series of [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|rock carvings]] depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings in [[:en:Dazu District|Dazu District]], [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]].]]
Another grouping found in certain Chinese depictions is the '''Ten Great Wisdom Kings''' (十大明王; ''Shí Dà Míngwáng''). The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping is from ''The Sutra of the Liturgy for Brilliant Contemplation of the Ten Wrathful Wisdom Kings of the Illusory Net of the Great Yoga Teachings'' (佛說幻化網大瑜伽教十忿怒明王大明觀想儀軌經; ''Fóshuō Huànhuàwǎng Dà yújiājiào Shífènnù Míngwáng Dàmíng Guānxiǎng Yíguǐ Jīng)''.{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} There are several different groupings of the ten Kings, which differ in the removal and addition of certain ''vidyārājas'', as well as attributing some Kings to different buddhas and bodhisattvas. In medieval and modern Chinese Buddhist practice, the Ten Kings are regularly invoked in repentance ceremonies, such as the [[:en:Liberation Rite of Water and Land|Liberation Rite of Water and Land]], where they are offered offerings and entreated to expel evil from the ritual platform.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Bloom |first1=Phillip Emmanual |date=2013 |title=Descent of the Deities: The Water-Land Retreat and the Transformation of the Visual Culture of Song-Dynasty (960–1279) Buddhism |id={{ProQuest|1422026705}} |oclc=864907811 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hong |first1=Tsai-Hsia |title=The Water-Land Dharma Function Platform Ritual and the Great Compassion Repentance Ritual |date=2005 |oclc=64281400 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref>
One version of the list of Ten Wisdom Kings are as follows:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}}
* Acala - Manifestation of Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of Vajrapani *Mahācakra - Manifestation of Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Manifestation of Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Manifestation of Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of Amitābha *Hayagrīva - Manifestation of Avalokiteśvara *[[Vajrahāsa]] (大笑明王; Ch. ''Dàxiào Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of Ākāśagarbha *Ucchuṣma (穢跡金剛明王; Ch. ''Huìjì Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Vajra Being of Impure Traces") - Manifestation of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Śakyamuni]] *Ucchuṣma (?) (火頭金剛明王; Ch. ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Fire-Headed Vajra Being") - Manifestation of Mahāvairocana{{efn|''Huìjì Jīngāng'' and ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng'' are sometimes considered to be different names for the same figure, but at times are also regarded as two separate deities.}}
Another version of the list identifies the ten Kings with different buddhas and bodhisattvas:
*Acala - Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin *Kuṇḍali - Amitābha *Trailokyavijaya - Vajrapāṇi *Mahācakra - Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Mañjuśrī *Hayagrīva - Avalokiteśvara *Vajrahāsa - Ākāśagarbha *[[Mahabala (Wisdom King)|Mahābala]] (大力明王; Ch, ''Dàlì Míngwáng'') - Śakyamuni
<gallery widths="184" heights="220" perrow="6" caption="[[:en:Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]] mural of the Ten Wisdom Kings in [[:zh:大云寺_(浑源)|Dayun Temple]] in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Datong|Datong]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]], [[:en:China|China]]"> File:Ming dynasty mural of Mahabala (大力明王; Dali Mingwang), one out of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Mahābala]] (大力明王; ''Dàlì Míngwáng'') File:Ming Dynasty mural of Hayagriva (馬頭觀音; 马头观音; Matou) and Acala (不動明王;不动明王; Budong), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]] (''Mǎtóu Guānyīn'') on the left and [[Acala]] (''Bùdòng Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Mahacakra (大輪明王; 大轮明王; Dalun Mingwang) and Yamantaka (大威德明王; Daweide Mingwang), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Mahācakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (''Dàlún Míngwáng'') on the left and [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]] (''Dàwēidé Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Aparajita (無能勝明王; 无能胜明王) and Padanaksipa (步擲明王;步掷明王), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparajita]] (''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng'') on the left and [[Padanaksipa]] (''Bùzhì Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Vajrahasa (大笑明王; Daxiao Mingwang) and Kundali (軍荼利明王; 军荼利明王; Juntuli Mingwang), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Vajrahāsa]] (''Dàxiào Míngwáng'') on the left and [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (''Jūntúlì Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming dynasty mural of Trailokyavijaya (降三世明王; Xiangsanshi Mingwang), one out of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (''Xiángsānshì Míngwáng'') </gallery>
===Others=== [[File:愛染明王, Rāgarāja, Kamakura period 2.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (''Aizen Myōō''), 13th century, Japan. [[:en:Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]]]
Other deities to whom the title ''vidyārāja'' is applied include:
* [[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (愛染明王; Ch. ''Àirǎn Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Aizen Myōō'') - A ''vidyaraja'' considered to transform worldly lust and sexual passion into spiritual awakening; manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrasattva|Vajrasattva]] and/or the buddha Vairochana.<ref>{{cite web |title=愛染明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/aizen.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref> * [[:en:Āṭavaka|Āṭavaka]] (大元帥明王; Ch. ''Dàyuánshuài Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daigensui Myōō'' or 大元明王, ''Daigen Myōō'') - A yaksha attendant of the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Vaiśravaṇa|Vaishravana]]. * [[Mahamayuri|Mahāmāyūrī]] (孔雀明王; Ch. ''Kǒngquè Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Kujaku Myōō'') - A Wisdom Queen (''vidyārājñī''); sometimes also classified as a bodhisattva. Unlike most other ''vidyārājas'', s/he is depicted with a benevolent expression. *Mahākrodharāja (大可畏明王; Ch. ''Dàkěwèi Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daikai Myōō'') - Attendant or manifestation of Amoghapasha (不空羂索観音; Ch. ''Bùkōng Juànsuǒ Guānyīn''; Jp. ''Fukū Kensaku/Kenjaku Kannon''), one of Avalokiteshvara's forms.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=89}}<ref>{{cite web |title=仏像がわかる！ バックナンバー４・明王部 |url=http://www5a.biglobe.ne.jp/~houon/butu-bk04.htm |website=Kōya-san Shingon-shū Hōon-in Official Website |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=不空大可畏明王央俱拾真言 |url=https://wisdombox.org/Mantra/15_t.pdf |website=JBox-智慧宝箧 |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref> *Sadākṣara (六字明王; Ch. ''Liùzì Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Rokuji Myōō'') - A deification of the Sadākṣara (Six-Letter) Sutra Ritual (六字経法; Jp. ''Rokuji-kyō hō''), a rite of subjugation focused on the [[Guanyin#Manifestations of Guanyin|six manifestations]] of Avalokiteshvara.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fuji |first1=Tatsuhiko |title=呪法全書 (Juhō Zensho) |date=2012 |publisher=Gakken Plus |isbn=978-4-0591-1008-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gi5jCwAAQBAJ&pg=PT150}}</ref> Unlike other Wisdom Kings but like Mahamayuri, he sports a gentle bodhisattva-like countenance and is shown with four or six arms and standing on one leg.<ref>{{cite web |title=円成庵 木造六字尊立像 |url=http://www.sumitomo.or.jp/html/culja/culja17/jp17029.htm |website=2017th year 度 文化財維持・修復事業助成 助成対象 |publisher=The Sumitomo Foundation|access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=木造六字明王立像 |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/kurashi/kosodate/bunka/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai/chokoku/rokujison_ritsuzo.html |website=Takamatsu City Official Website |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=六字明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/rokuji.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref>
== Examples == Examples of depictions of the Eight Wisdom Kings can be found at:
* Cliff reliefs and rock carvings at [[Shizhongshan Grottoes]]<sup>[[:zh:石钟山石窟|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Jianchuan County|Jianchuan]], [[:en:Yunnan|Yunnan]] * Statues in the [[Datong Guanyin Hall]]<sup>[[:zh:大同观音堂|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Datong|Datong]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] *Frescos in the [[:en:Pagoda|Pagoda]] at [[Jueshan Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:觉山寺|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Lingqiu County|Lingqiu]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]]
Examples of depictions of the Ten Wisdom Kings can be found at:
* Rock carvings at the [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|Dazu Rock Carving sites]] in [[:en:Dazu District|Dazu]], [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]] * Statues in [[:en:Shuanglin Temple|Shuanglin Temple]] near [[:en:Pingyao|Pingyao]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Statues in [[Shuilu Nunnery]]<sup>[[:zh:水陆庵|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Lantian County|Lantian]], [[:en:Xi'an|Xi'an]] * Frescos in [[:en:Qinglong Temple (Jishan County)|Qinglong Temple]] in [[:en:Jishan County|Jishan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Yong'an Temple (Hunyuan County)|Yong'an Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:永安寺_(浑源)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Yunlin Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:云林寺_(阳高)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Yanggao County|Yanggao]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Pilu Temple]]<sup>[zh]</sup> in [[:en:Shijiazhuang|Shijiazhuang]], [[:en:Hebei|Hebei]] * Frescos in [[Dayun Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:大云寺_(浑源)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * [[:en:Water and Land Ritual paintings|Water and Land Ritual paintings]] from various temples, such as [[Baoning Temple (Shanxi)|Baoning Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:宝宁寺|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Youyu County|Youyu]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] (Currently kept in the [[:en:Shanxi Museum|Shanxi Museum]]) * Documents and carvings from the [[:en:Mogao Caves|Mogao Caves]] near [[:en:Dunhuang|Dunhuang]], [[:en:Gansu|Gansu]]

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[bn:বিদ্যারাজ]][[en:Wisdom King]][[es:Reyes de la sabiduría]][[eu:Vidyarāja]][[fr:Vidyaraja]][[hu:Bölcsességkirályok]][[id:Vidyārāja]][[ja:明王]][[ko:명왕]][[lt:Vidjaradža]][[pl:Widjaradża]][[ro:Regii înțelepciunii]][[ru:Видья-раджа]][[ta:வித்யாராஜாக்கள்]][[th:วิทยาราช]][[zh:明王]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q855113]] Wikidata name: Wisdom King [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:22, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Wrathful deity in East Asian Buddhism}} {{Vajrayana}}
A '''Wisdom King''' ([[:en:Sanskrit|Sanskrit]]: विद्याराज; [[:en:International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration|IAST]]: ''Vidyārāja'', {{cjkv|p=Míngwáng|c=明王|r=Myōō}}) is a type of [[:en:Wrathful deities|wrathful deity]] in [[:en:East Asian Buddhism|East Asian Buddhism]].
Whereas the Sanskrit name is translated literally as "wisdom / knowledge king(s)," the term ''[[:en:Vidya (philosophy)|vidyā]]'' in [[:en:Vajrayana Buddhism|Vajrayana Buddhism]] is also specifically used to denote [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]];<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Toganoo |first1=Shozui Makoto |title=The Symbol-System of Shingon Buddhism (1) |journal=Journal of Esoteric Buddhism – Mikkyō Bunka |date=1971 |pages=91, 86 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jeb1947/1971/96/1971_96_L95/_pdf/-char/ja}}</ref> the term may thus also be rendered "mantra king(s)."{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Mack|2006|p=298}} ''Vidyā'' is translated in Chinese with the character (lit. "bright, radiant", figuratively "knowledge(able), wisdom, wise"), leading to a wide array of alternative translations such as "bright king(s)" or "radiant king(s)". A similar Category of fierce deities known as [[:en:Heruka|Heruka]]s are found in [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan Buddhism]].
The female counterparts of Wisdom Kings are known as '''Wisdom Queens''' (Sanskrit (IAST): ''Vidyārājñī'', Chinese: 明妃, ''Míngfēi'', Japanese: ''Myōhi'').
===Development=== [[File:Dazu-Baoding Shan-304-No21-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|300px|Carved cliff relief of [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamantaka]] (''Dàwēidé Míngwáng)'', one out of a set depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings, at the [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|Dazu Rock Carvings]] in [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]]. 12th century. ]] ''Vidyārājas'', as their name suggests, are originally conceived of as the guardians and personifications of esoteric wisdom (''vidyā''), namely [[:en:Mantra|Mantra]] and [[:en:Dharani|Dharani]]s. They were seen as embodying the mystic power contained in these sacred utterances.{{sfnp|Haneda|2018|pp=25-27}}{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=116}}
During the early stages of esoteric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, many of the deities that would become known as ''vidyārājas'' (a term that only came into use around the late 7th-early 8th century{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=90}}) were mainly seen as attendants of [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]]s who were invoked for specific ends such as the removal of misfortune and obstacles to [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. They personified certain attributes of these bodhisattvas such as their wisdom or the power of their voices and were held to perform various tasks such as gathering together sentient beings to whom the bodhisattva preaches, subjugating unruly elements, or protecting adherents of Buddhism.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13, 64-65}} Eventually, these divinities became objects of veneration in their own right; no longer necessarily paired with a bodhisattva, they became considered as the manifestations of the bodhisattvas themselves and/or of [[:en:Buddhahood|buddhas]], who are believed to assume terrifying forms as a [[:en:Upaya|means]] to save sentient beings out of [[:en:Karuṇā|compassion]] for them.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=13}} A belief prevalent in the Japanese tradition known as the ''sanrinjin'' (三輪身, "bodies of the three wheels") theory for instance posits that five Wisdom Kings are the fierce incarnations (教令輪身, ''kyōryōrin-shin'', lit. "embodiments of the wheel of injunction") of the [[:en:Five Tathāgatas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]], who appear both as gentle bodhisattvas who teach the Dharma through compassion and as terrifying ''vidyārājas'' who teach through fear, shocking nonbelievers into faith.{{sfnp|Baroni|2002|p=100}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|2006|p=56}}<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_H5p-Fqkuz8C&pg=PA120|title=昭和新纂国訳大蔵経 解説部第1巻 (Shōwa shinsan Kokuyaku Daizōkyō: Kaisetsu, vol. 1)|date=1930|publisher=Tōhō Shuppan|pages=120|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=三輪身|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E8%BC%AA%E8%BA%AB-71616|access-date=2020-11-28|website=コトバンク (kotobank)|language=ja}}</ref>
[[File:Indian Museum Sculpture - Manjusri, 10c, Kurkihar (9220688818).jpg|thumb|150px|[[Manjushri]] with Yamāntaka, from Kurkihar ([[:en:Bihar|Bihar]]), currently at the [[:en:Indian Museum, Kolkata|Indian Museum]] in [[:en:Kolkata|Kolkata]]. 10th century.|left]] The evolution of the ''vidyārāja'' will be illustrated here by the deity [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]], one of the earliest Buddhist wrathful deities. In the 6th century text ''[[:en:Manjushrimulakalpa|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa]]'', Yamāntaka is portrayed as the oath-bound servant of the bodhisattva [[Manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] who assembles all beings from across the world to hear the Buddha's preaching and vanquishes (and converts) those who are hostile to Buddhism; at the same time, Yamāntaka is also the personification of Mañjuśrī's dharani, the benefits of which are identical to his abilities.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=64-67}} He was also commonly depicted in statuary along with Mañjuśrī as a diminutive [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]]-like attendant figure.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=68-81}}
[[File:Dai Itoku Myoo Yamantaka Toji.JPG|thumb|Yamāntaka (''Daiitoku Myōō''), at [[Tō-ji]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (13th or 14th century). ]] Later, as Yamāntaka and similar subordinates of various bodhisattvas (e.g. [[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]], who was associated with [[:en:Avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]]) became fully independent deities, they began to be portrayed by themselves and increasingly acquired iconographic attributes specific to each. Yamāntaka for instance is commonly shown with six heads, arms, and legs and riding or standing on a [[:en:Water Buffalo|buffalo]] [[:en:Vahana|mount]].{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} The status and function of these deities have shifted from being minor emissaries who gather together and intimidate recalcitrant beings to being intimately involved in the primary task of esoteric Buddhism: the transformation of passions and ignorance (''[[:en:Avidyā (Buddhism)|avidyā]]'') into compassion and wisdom.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=155}} As a result of this development, the relationship between Mañjuśrī and Yamāntaka was recontextualized such that Yamāntaka is now considered to be the incarnation of Mañjuśrī himself (so the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|Mañjuśrī-nāma-samgīti]]'').{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=163-175}} Eventually, in the ''sanrinjin'' interpretation of Japanese esoteric Buddhism, both Yamāntaka and Mañjuśrī - under the name 'Vajratīkṣṇa' (Japanese: 金剛利菩薩, ''Kongōri Bosatsu'')<ref>{{cite web |title=3. 両界曼荼羅（りょうかいまんだら） |url=https://ermjp.com/j/temple/mandara/manda/oshie/oshie7.html |website=Shingon-shū Sennyū-ji-ha Jōdo-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Vajratiksna |url=https://english-tibetan-dictionary.tumblr.com/post/59668575364/vajratiksna |website=English Tibetan Dictionary Online |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref> - became classified as avatars of the buddha [[Amitābha|Amitābha]].<ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A7%E5%A8%81%E5%BE%B3%E6%98%8E%E7%8E%8B-90795 |website=コトバンク (Kotobank) |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=大威徳明王 |url=http://www.ict.ne.jp/~jofukuji/daiitoku.html |website=Shingon-shū Buzan-ha Kōki-zan Jōfuku-ji Official Website |access-date=2021-09-28}}</ref>
Other Wisdom Kings followed a more or less similar development. Hayagrīva, for example, was originally the horse-headed incarnation of the [[:en:Hinduism|Hindu]] god [[:en:Vishnu|Vishnu]] which was adopted into Buddhism as Avalokiteśvara's attendant (although unlike the Hindu [[:en:Hayagriva|Hayagrīva]], the Buddhist figure was never portrayed with a horse's head, instead being depicted like Yamāntaka as a yaksha who may have a miniature horse head emerging from his hair).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=85-91}} Eventually, as Hayagrīva increasingly rose to prominence, the distinction between him and his superior became increasingly blurred so that he ultimately turned into one of Avalokiteśvara's many guises in both China and Japan.{{sfnp|Chandra|1988|pp=29-31}} One of the more famous ''vidyārājas'', [[Acala]] (Acalanātha), was originally an acolyte or messenger of the buddha [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]] before he was interpreted as Vairocana's fierce aspect or ''kyōryōrin-shin'' in the Japanese tradition.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=120-123}} (In Nepal and Tibet, meanwhile, he is instead identified as the incarnation of either Mañjuśrī or the buddha [[Akshobhya|Akṣobhya]].{{sfnp|Pal|1974|p=6}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Acala, The Buddhist Protector|url=https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38011|access-date=2020-11-28|website=Metropolitan Museum of Art}}</ref>{{sfnp|Jha|1993|pp=35–36}}<ref name=":22">{{Cite web|title=Sacred Visions: Early Paintings from Central Tibet - Achala|url=https://www.asianart.com/exhibitions/svision/i22.html|access-date=2020-11-28|website=www.asianart.com}}</ref>)
==Iconography== {{multiple image | direction = vertical | width = 200 | footer = | image1 = Kongosanmaiin tahoto interior.jpg | caption1 = Statues of the [[:en:Five Tathāgatas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]] (五智如来, ''Gochi Nyorai'') at [[:en:Kongō Sanmai-in|Kongō Sanmai-in]] in [[:en:Mount Kōya|Mount Kōya]], Japan. Kamakura period (13th century). Clockwise starting from the front right: [[Amoghasiddhi]], [[Akshobhya]], [[:en:Ratnasambhava|Ratnasambhava]], and [[Amitābha|Amitabha]]. [[:en:Vairochana|Vairochana]] is at the center. | image2 = The Five Wisdom Kings.jpg | caption2 = The Five Wisdom Kings (五大明王, ''Godai Myōō''). Clockwise starting from the top right: [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]], [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]], [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]], and [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]]. [[Acala]] is at the center. }}
The iconography of Buddhist wrathful deities are usually considered to be derived from both [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] imagery and [[:en:Shaivism|Shaivite]] iconography, specifically from the wrathful forms of the Hindu god [[:en:Shiva|Shiva]] (e.g. [[:en:Bhairava|Bhairava]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=330}}<ref>{{Cite web|last=Van Hartingsveldt|first=Michael|date=2018-09-21|title=With the Wrath of a Serpent: The Propagation of Gundari Myо̄о̄ Iconography|url=https://www.buddhistdoor.net/features/with-the-wrath-of-a-serpent-the-propagation-of-gudari-myoo-iconography|access-date=2021-09-25|website=Buddhistdoor Global}}</ref>
Wisdom Kings are usually represented as fierce-looking, often with blue or black skin and multiple heads, arms, and legs. They hold various weapons in their hands and are sometimes adorned with [[Mundamala|skulls]], [[Shiva#Attributes|snakes or animal skins]] and wreathed in flames. This fiery aura is symbolically interpreted as the fire that purifies the practitioner and transforms one's [[:en:Kleshas (Buddhism)|passions]] into awakening, the so-called "fire ''[[Samadhi#Samādhi|samadhi]]''" (火生三昧, Japanese: ''kashō-zanmai'').{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|p=117}}
Certain ''vidyārājas'' bear attributes that reflect [[Decline of Buddhism in the Indian subcontinent#Religious competition|the historical rivalry]] between Hinduism and Buddhism. For instance, the Wisdom King [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] is shown defeating and trampling on the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Maheshvara|Maheśvara]] (one of the Buddhist analogues to Shiva) and his consort Umā ([[:en:Parvati|Pārvatī]]).{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|pp=178-187}} A commentary on the ''[[:en:Mahavairocana Tantra|Mahavairocana Tantra]]'' by the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] monk [[Yi Xing]] meanwhile attributes the taming of Maheśvara to another ''vidyārāja'', Acala.{{sfnp|Faure|2015a|pp=124-125}} Acala himself is sometimes shown trampling on an elephant-headed demon/deity [[Kangiten#Historical development and literature|who may share a common origin]] with the Hindu [[:en:Ganesha|Ganesha]] named Vighnarāja (the "Lord of Obstacles") in [[:en:Tibetan art|Tibetan art]].{{sfnp|Faure|2015b|pp=47, 94–98}}
==List of Wisdom Kings== ===The Five Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese]] and Japanese ([[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon]] and [[:en:Tendai|Tendai]]) esoteric Buddhism, the '''Five Great Wisdom Kings''' (五大明王, Jp. ''Godai Myōō''; Ch. ''Wǔ Dà Míngwáng''), also known as the '''Five Guardian Kings''', are a group of ''vidyārājas'' who are considered to be both the fierce emanations of the [[:en:Five Wisdom Buddhas|Five Wisdom Buddhas]] and the guardians of Buddhist doctrine.{{sfnp|De Visser|1928|pp=143-151}}<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vilbar |first1=Sinéad |title=Kings of Brightness in Japanese Esoteric Buddhist Art |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/kibr/hd_kibr.htm |website=The Metropolitan Museum of Art |access-date=2021-10-01 |date=October 2013}}</ref> Organized according to the five directions (the [[:en:Cardinal direction|four cardinal points]] plus the center), the Five Kings are usually defined as follows:
* [[Acala|Acala / Acalanātha]] (不動明王; Jp. ''Fudō Myōō''; Ch. 不動明王, ''Bùdòng Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Vairocana|Mahāvairocana]], associated with the center * [[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (降三世明王; Jp. ''Gōzanze Myōō''; Ch. ''Xiángsānshì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Akshobhya|Akshobhya]], associated with the east * [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali / Amṛtakuṇḍalin]] (軍荼利明王, Jp. ''Gundari Myōō''; Ch. ''Jūntúlì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[:en:Ratnasambhava|Ratnasambhava]], associated with the south * [[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (大威徳明王; Jp. ''Daiitoku Myōō''; Ch. ''Dàwēidé Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amitābha]], associated with the west * [[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]] (金剛夜叉明王, Jp. ''Kongōyasha Myōō''; Ch. ''Jīngāng Yèchā Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of [[Amoghasiddhi]], associated with the north in the Shingon school ** [[:en:Ucchusma|Ucchuṣma]] (烏枢沙摩明王; Jp. ''Ususama Myōō''; Ch. ''Wūshūshāmó Míngwáng'') - Associated with the north in the Tendai school<ref>{{cite web |title=五大尊 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/5daison/index.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudō (Ryukō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-01}}</ref>
{| align="center" border="0" cellspacing="5" | |align = "center"|[[:en:Vajrayakṣa|Vajrayakṣa]] ''or'' [[:en:Ucchusma|Ucchuṣma]] (north) | |- |align = "center"|[[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]] (west) |align = "center"|[[Acala]] (center) |align = "center"|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (east) |- | |align = "center"|[[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (south) | |}
===The Eight Wisdom Kings=== In [[:en:Chinese Buddhism|Chinese Buddhism]], the '''Eight Great Wisdom Kings''' (八大明王; pinyin: ''Bā Dà Míngwáng''), is another grouping of Wisdom Kings that is depicted in statues, mural art and paintings. The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping of eight is the ''Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa'', the Chinese translation of which (大方廣菩薩藏文殊舍利根本儀軌經; ''Dà fāngguǎng Púsà Zàng Wénshūshèlì Gēnběn Yíguǐ Jīng'', lit. "The Fundamental Ordinance of Mañjuśrī") in about 980-1000 CE is attributed to the monk Tianxizai, who is possibly the north Indian [[:en:Shantideva|Shantideva]].{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} Each of the Wisdom Kings correspond to one of the [[Eight Great Bodhisattvas]][[:zh:八大菩萨|<sup>zh]</sup>]] in Chinese Buddhism as well as to a specific compass direction.
The Eight Wisdom Kings, with exceptions in certain lists, are usually defined as:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} * Acala - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin|Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin]], associated with the north-east * Kuṇḍali - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Ākāśagarbha|Ākāśagarbha]], associated with the north-west * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrapani|Vajrapāṇi]], associated with the south-east *[[Mahācakra]] (大輪明王; Ch. ''Dàlún Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[Maitreya]], associated with the south-west *[[Padanakṣipa]] (步擲明王; Ch. ''Bùzhì Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], associated with the north *[[Aparājita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (無能勝明王; Ch. ''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng)'' - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Kṣitigarbha]], associated with the south *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, associated with the east *Hayagrīva (馬頭觀音; Ch. ''Mǎtóu Guānyīn'') - Manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]] ([[Kannon|Guanyin]]), associated with the west
{| align="center" border="0" cellspacing="5" |align = "center"|[[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (north-west) |align = "center"|[[Padanakṣipa]] (north) |align = "center"|[[Acala]] (north-east) |- |align = "center"|[[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]] (west) | |align = "center"|[[:en:Yamāntaka|Yamāntaka]] (east) |- |align = "center"|[[Mahacakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (south-west) |align = "center"|[[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparājita]] (south) |align = "center"|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (south-east) |}
=== The Ten Wisdom Kings === [[File:Dazu 2007 774.jpg|thumb|320px|The Wisdom Kings [[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparajita]] (''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng''; left), [[Mahācakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (''Dàlún Míngwáng''; center), and [[Padanakṣipa]] (''Bùzhì Míngwáng''; right). Part of a series of [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|rock carvings]] depicting the Ten Wisdom Kings in [[:en:Dazu District|Dazu District]], [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]], [[:en:China|China]].]]
Another grouping found in certain Chinese depictions is the '''Ten Great Wisdom Kings''' (十大明王; ''Shí Dà Míngwáng''). The acknowledged canonical source of the grouping is from ''The Sutra of the Liturgy for Brilliant Contemplation of the Ten Wrathful Wisdom Kings of the Illusory Net of the Great Yoga Teachings'' (佛說幻化網大瑜伽教十忿怒明王大明觀想儀軌經; ''Fóshuō Huànhuàwǎng Dà yújiājiào Shífènnù Míngwáng Dàmíng Guānxiǎng Yíguǐ Jīng)''.{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}} There are several different groupings of the ten Kings, which differ in the removal and addition of certain ''vidyārājas'', as well as attributing some Kings to different buddhas and bodhisattvas. In medieval and modern Chinese Buddhist practice, the Ten Kings are regularly invoked in repentance ceremonies, such as the [[:en:Liberation Rite of Water and Land|Liberation Rite of Water and Land]], where they are offered offerings and entreated to expel evil from the ritual platform.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Bloom |first1=Phillip Emmanual |date=2013 |title=Descent of the Deities: The Water-Land Retreat and the Transformation of the Visual Culture of Song-Dynasty (960–1279) Buddhism |id={{ProQuest|1422026705}} |oclc=864907811 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hong |first1=Tsai-Hsia |title=The Water-Land Dharma Function Platform Ritual and the Great Compassion Repentance Ritual |date=2005 |oclc=64281400 }}{{pn|date=June 2023}}</ref>
One version of the list of Ten Wisdom Kings are as follows:{{sfnp|Howard|2002|pp=92–107}}
* Acala - Manifestation of Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin * Trailokyavijaya - Manifestation of Vajrapani *Mahācakra - Manifestation of Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Manifestation of Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Manifestation of Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Manifestation of Amitābha *Hayagrīva - Manifestation of Avalokiteśvara *[[Vajrahāsa]] (大笑明王; Ch. ''Dàxiào Míngwáng'') - Manifestation of Ākāśagarbha *Ucchuṣma (穢跡金剛明王; Ch. ''Huìjì Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Vajra Being of Impure Traces") - Manifestation of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Śakyamuni]] *Ucchuṣma (?) (火頭金剛明王; Ch. ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng Míngwáng'', lit. "Fire-Headed Vajra Being") - Manifestation of Mahāvairocana{{efn|''Huìjì Jīngāng'' and ''Huǒtóu Jīngāng'' are sometimes considered to be different names for the same figure, but at times are also regarded as two separate deities.}}
Another version of the list identifies the ten Kings with different buddhas and bodhisattvas:
*Acala - Sarvanivāraṇaviṣkambhin *Kuṇḍali - Amitābha *Trailokyavijaya - Vajrapāṇi *Mahācakra - Maitreya *Padanakṣipa - Samantabhadra *Aparājita - Kṣitigarbha *Yamāntaka - Mañjuśrī *Hayagrīva - Avalokiteśvara *Vajrahāsa - Ākāśagarbha *[[Mahabala (Wisdom King)|Mahābala]] (大力明王; Ch, ''Dàlì Míngwáng'') - Śakyamuni
<gallery widths="184" heights="220" perrow="6" caption="[[:en:Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]] mural of the Ten Wisdom Kings in [[:zh:大云寺_(浑源)|Dayun Temple]] in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Datong|Datong]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]], [[:en:China|China]]"> File:Ming dynasty mural of Mahabala (大力明王; Dali Mingwang), one out of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Mahābala]] (大力明王; ''Dàlì Míngwáng'') File:Ming Dynasty mural of Hayagriva (馬頭觀音; 马头观音; Matou) and Acala (不動明王;不动明王; Budong), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[:en:Hayagriva (Buddhism)|Hayagrīva]] (''Mǎtóu Guānyīn'') on the left and [[Acala]] (''Bùdòng Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Mahacakra (大輪明王; 大轮明王; Dalun Mingwang) and Yamantaka (大威德明王; Daweide Mingwang), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Mahācakra (Wisdom King)|Mahācakra]] (''Dàlún Míngwáng'') on the left and [[:en:Yamantaka|Yamāntaka]] (''Dàwēidé Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Aparajita (無能勝明王; 无能胜明王) and Padanaksipa (步擲明王;步掷明王), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Aparajita (Wisdom King)|Aparajita]] (''Wúnéngshēng Míngwáng'') on the left and [[Padanaksipa]] (''Bùzhì Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming Dynasty mural of Vajrahasa (大笑明王; Daxiao Mingwang) and Kundali (軍荼利明王; 军荼利明王; Juntuli Mingwang), two of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[Vajrahāsa]] (''Dàxiào Míngwáng'') on the left and [[:en:Kuṇḍali|Kuṇḍali]] (''Jūntúlì Míngwáng'') on the right File:Ming dynasty mural of Trailokyavijaya (降三世明王; Xiangsanshi Mingwang), one out of Ten Wisdom Kings (十大明王), in Dayun Temple (浑源大云寺), Hunyuan, Datong, Shanxi, China.jpg|[[:en:Trailokyavijaya|Trailokyavijaya]] (''Xiángsānshì Míngwáng'') </gallery>
===Others=== [[File:愛染明王, Rāgarāja, Kamakura period 2.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (''Aizen Myōō''), 13th century, Japan. [[:en:Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]]]
Other deities to whom the title ''vidyārāja'' is applied include:
* [[:en:Rāgarāja|Rāgarāja]] (愛染明王; Ch. ''Àirǎn Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Aizen Myōō'') - A ''vidyaraja'' considered to transform worldly lust and sexual passion into spiritual awakening; manifestation of the bodhisattva [[:en:Vajrasattva|Vajrasattva]] and/or the buddha Vairochana.<ref>{{cite web |title=愛染明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/aizen.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref> * [[:en:Āṭavaka|Āṭavaka]] (大元帥明王; Ch. ''Dàyuánshuài Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daigensui Myōō'' or 大元明王, ''Daigen Myōō'') - A yaksha attendant of the [[:en:Deva (Buddhism)|deva]] [[:en:Vaiśravaṇa|Vaishravana]]. * [[Mahamayuri|Mahāmāyūrī]] (孔雀明王; Ch. ''Kǒngquè Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Kujaku Myōō'') - A Wisdom Queen (''vidyārājñī''); sometimes also classified as a bodhisattva. Unlike most other ''vidyārājas'', s/he is depicted with a benevolent expression. *Mahākrodharāja (大可畏明王; Ch. ''Dàkěwèi Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Daikai Myōō'') - Attendant or manifestation of Amoghapasha (不空羂索観音; Ch. ''Bùkōng Juànsuǒ Guānyīn''; Jp. ''Fukū Kensaku/Kenjaku Kannon''), one of Avalokiteshvara's forms.{{sfnp|Linrothe|1999|p=89}}<ref>{{cite web |title=仏像がわかる！ バックナンバー４・明王部 |url=http://www5a.biglobe.ne.jp/~houon/butu-bk04.htm |website=Kōya-san Shingon-shū Hōon-in Official Website |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=不空大可畏明王央俱拾真言 |url=https://wisdombox.org/Mantra/15_t.pdf |website=JBox-智慧宝箧 |access-date=2021-10-02}}</ref> *Sadākṣara (六字明王; Ch. ''Liùzì Míngwáng''; Jp. ''Rokuji Myōō'') - A deification of the Sadākṣara (Six-Letter) Sutra Ritual (六字経法; Jp. ''Rokuji-kyō hō''), a rite of subjugation focused on the [[Guanyin#Manifestations of Guanyin|six manifestations]] of Avalokiteshvara.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fuji |first1=Tatsuhiko |title=呪法全書 (Juhō Zensho) |date=2012 |publisher=Gakken Plus |isbn=978-4-0591-1008-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gi5jCwAAQBAJ&pg=PT150}}</ref> Unlike other Wisdom Kings but like Mahamayuri, he sports a gentle bodhisattva-like countenance and is shown with four or six arms and standing on one leg.<ref>{{cite web |title=円成庵 木造六字尊立像 |url=http://www.sumitomo.or.jp/html/culja/culja17/jp17029.htm |website=2017th year 度 文化財維持・修復事業助成 助成対象 |publisher=The Sumitomo Foundation|access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=木造六字明王立像 |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/kurashi/kosodate/bunka/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai/chokoku/rokujison_ritsuzo.html |website=Takamatsu City Official Website |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=六字明王 |url=http://tobifudo.jp/butuzo/myoou/rokuji.html |website=Flying Deity Tobifudo (Ryūkō-zan Shōbō-in Official Website) |access-date=2021-10-16}}</ref>
== Examples == Examples of depictions of the Eight Wisdom Kings can be found at:
* Cliff reliefs and rock carvings at [[Shizhongshan Grottoes]]<sup>[[:zh:石钟山石窟|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Jianchuan County|Jianchuan]], [[:en:Yunnan|Yunnan]] * Statues in the [[Datong Guanyin Hall]]<sup>[[:zh:大同观音堂|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Datong|Datong]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] *Frescos in the [[:en:Pagoda|Pagoda]] at [[Jueshan Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:觉山寺|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Lingqiu County|Lingqiu]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]]
Examples of depictions of the Ten Wisdom Kings can be found at:
* Rock carvings at the [[:en:Dazu Rock Carvings|Dazu Rock Carving sites]] in [[:en:Dazu District|Dazu]], [[:en:Chongqing|Chongqing]] * Statues in [[:en:Shuanglin Temple|Shuanglin Temple]] near [[:en:Pingyao|Pingyao]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Statues in [[Shuilu Nunnery]]<sup>[[:zh:水陆庵|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Lantian County|Lantian]], [[:en:Xi'an|Xi'an]] * Frescos in [[:en:Qinglong Temple (Jishan County)|Qinglong Temple]] in [[:en:Jishan County|Jishan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Yong'an Temple (Hunyuan County)|Yong'an Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:永安寺_(浑源)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Yunlin Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:云林寺_(阳高)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Yanggao County|Yanggao]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * Frescos in [[Pilu Temple]]<sup>[zh]</sup> in [[:en:Shijiazhuang|Shijiazhuang]], [[:en:Hebei|Hebei]] * Frescos in [[Dayun Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:大云寺_(浑源)|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Hunyuan County|Hunyuan]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] * [[:en:Water and Land Ritual paintings|Water and Land Ritual paintings]] from various temples, such as [[Baoning Temple (Shanxi)|Baoning Temple]]<sup>[[:zh:宝宁寺|[zh]]]</sup> in [[:en:Youyu County|Youyu]], [[:en:Shanxi|Shanxi]] (Currently kept in the [[:en:Shanxi Museum|Shanxi Museum]]) * Documents and carvings from the [[:en:Mogao Caves|Mogao Caves]] near [[:en:Dunhuang|Dunhuang]], [[:en:Gansu|Gansu]]
